observation: fMRI evidence (Constantinescu, O'Reilly & Behrens 2016, Science) shows hexagonal grid-cell-like coding in entorhinal cortex for entirely non-spatial, abstract 2D conceptual spaces, replicated within-session and across a week.
claim: The brain reuses spatial-navigation neural machinery for abstract knowledge organization, which is direct neuroscientific support for a 'proximity = relatedness' spatial UI metaphor.
mechanism: Grid cells implement a general relational/structural code (vector computation over whichever space is being structured), not a literally spatial-only one.

implications.text: A spatial view where proximity encodes relatedness has a genuine neural analogue, supporting investment in FT-spatial-view as more than a metaphor.

observation: Cockburn & McKenzie (2002, CHI) directly compared physical, 2D, 2.5D and 3D virtual document layouts and found retrieval was slower in 3D than 2D, and slowest in 3D virtual vs. physical.
claim: Adding a third (depth) dimension to a spatial UI for its own sake costs retrieval speed rather than helping, unless the extra dimension encodes real, usable structure.
mechanism: 3D virtual layouts lack the vestibular/physical cues (leaning, walking) that ground 3D spatial memory in the real world, so the added dimension is pure navigation overhead.

implications.text: Do not use literal Z-axis depth/3D camera movement to encode 'importance' in the spatial view; use pseudo-depth (layering, opacity) instead.

observation: Cockburn, Karlson & Bederson (2008, ACM Computing Surveys) synthesize dozens of studies: overview+detail reliably supports spatial orientation/stable mental maps at the cost of split attention; pure zooming gives continuous transitions but costs orientation; focus+context is a wash, often confusing for novices.
claim: A persistent overview (minimap) alongside a zoomed detail view outperforms relying on zoom trajectory alone for keeping users oriented.
mechanism: Spatially separate global-context and local-focus views let users maintain a stable mental map that pure temporal zoom transitions erode.

implications.text: Default to overview+detail (persistent 'you are here' minimap) once a spatial view exists, rather than trusting zoom trajectory alone.

observation: 'Desert fog' is a named, documented failure mode where a zoomed/panned view shares no recognizable content with the prior view, leaving the user unable to reconstruct location; documented mitigations are a home button, overview map, recenter affordance, and persistent landmarks/labels.
claim: Every level/scale transition needs an explicit orientation anchor (home control, persistent landmark) or users lose their place.
mechanism: Without a visible element that survives the scale change, there is no cue bridging the before/after views.

implications.text: Provide a fixed, always-reachable home control and keep the L0 gist visible as a persistent header/breadcrumb at every zoom level.

observation: Force-directed graph views degrade into unreadable 'hairballs' past a few hundred nodes; convergent practitioner experience (Obsidian community, knowledge-graph HCI research) says the global graph is a diagnostic at best, and the useful daily view is a local/ego-centered graph.
claim: A literal force-directed 'graph of everything' should not be the primary spatial view once content scales; a local/ego view scoped to the current document is the usable default.
mechanism: Edge/node density beyond a few hundred items overwhelms visual parsing regardless of layout algorithm quality.

implications.text: Default the spatial view to a local/ego-centered graph (current document + immediate neighbors), with any global view as an occasional filterable overlay, not the primary surface.

observation: Misue, Eades, Lai & Sugiyama (1995) formalized 'mental map preservation' for dynamic graphs; follow-up empirical work found users track updated graphs faster/more accurately when relative node positions are preserved across redraws, even at some cost to layout aesthetics.
claim: When the spatial/tree view updates (new content, regeneration), relative node position should be preserved rather than re-optimized from scratch.
mechanism: Stability of relative position, not layout optimality, is what lets users retain orientation across changes.

implications.text: Layout function for the spatial view must preserve prior relative node positions across regeneration, not just optimize the new layout.

observation: Kevin Lynch's five urban-legibility elements (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks; The Image of the City, 1960) are proposed as a design vocabulary for knowledge-space UIs, but this transfer from urban design to abstract information spaces is by analogy, not separately tested.
claim: A legible spatial view needs a path (how you got here), edges (legible boundaries), districts (visually distinct topic regions), nodes (junctions), and landmarks (recognizable-by-shape references) — but this checklist is an assumed transfer, not an evidenced one for non-geographic spaces.
mechanism: Imageability in physical environments comes from consistent, recognizable structural elements; the hypothesis is this generalizes to abstract knowledge spaces.
population: general (urban-design theory, applied by analogy to infovis/games/VR)
context: theoretical framework, not tested in knowledge-space UI

implications.text: Use Lynch's five elements as a design checklist for the future spatial view, but treat it as an untested hypothesis pending Riemann-specific validation.

observation: Embedding-based 'maps of documents' (UMAP/t-SNE 2D projections, e.g. Nomic Atlas) are the closest existing analogue to an abstraction-tree spatial view, but UMAP/t-SNE preserve local neighborhood structure much better than global distances — two clusters that look close are not reliably more related than two that look far apart.
claim: If node position in the spatial view is ever derived from raw embedding projection, 2D distance between distant clusters must not be presented as meaningful relatedness.
mechanism: This is textbook dimensionality-reduction math, not a contested empirical finding: only within-cluster proximity is trustworthy in a 2D UMAP/t-SNE projection.
context: known limitation of UMAP/t-SNE, applied to Riemann's design

implications.text: Keep node layout driven by the tree's own parent/child structure (honest semantics) rather than raw embedding projection, or visually distinguish trustworthy (in-cluster) from untrustworthy (cross-cluster) proximity.

observation: Data Mountain (Robertson et al. 1998, UIST) found that letting users place web-page thumbnails at arbitrary positions on a 2D/3D plane produced faster, better-retained retrieval than a conventional favorites list.
claim: Self-chosen or system-assigned spatial position functions as a usable retrieval cue for documents, distinct from list-based navigation.
mechanism: Spatial position recruits an additional (spatial) memory channel beyond the semantic/textual one a plain list relies on.

implications.text: A stable spatial position for documents/nodes (not re-randomized) is a legitimate retrieval aid worth preserving across sessions, reinforcing FT-stable-layout.
